title: For the life of the world
word: For the life of the world
hook: Alexander Schmemann: humans are priests of creation, offering the world back in thanks

segments.voice: Yesterday, Karl Rahner: God met in plain moments nobody sees. Your line was mystic in the ordinary.

Before a meal, some families go quiet for a moment. A hand reaches for another hand. Someone says a few words of thanks, and then the dishes are passed and the noise comes back. Alexander Schmemann, an Orthodox priest and teacher, thought that small pause was a key to the whole of life. He wrote a short book about it, and he took its title from the Gospel of John: For the Life of the World.

Schmemann starts with something basic. People are hungry. We eat to live, and we stay hungry for more than food. In Genesis, he notices, the world first comes to humans as something to eat: a garden full of fruit, given as a gift, and God sees that it's good. So what are humans for? Schmemann's answer: we are the ones who can bless. Every creature eats. Humans can receive the world, give thanks to God for it, and offer it back. He calls this the priestly role of every person: a priest of creation. Not a job title. A way of holding things. When the thanks goes missing, the world doesn't stop being good. We just start treating it as stuff to use up. That's where the title comes in. In John, Jesus says: "the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world." At the heart of Orthodox worship is the Divine Liturgy, and at its heart is the Eucharist, a Greek word meaning thanksgiving. Christians understand what happens at that table in different ways, as this path has seen, and it ranks none of them. For Schmemann, the Eucharist shows what all of life is meant to be: received, blessed, offered back. The first letter to Timothy says it plainly: "every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving." So grace before a meal isn't a pause before real life. In Schmemann's eyes, it's real life in miniature, at a kitchen table.

If there's something near you to eat or drink, a glass of water, an apple, a cup of coffee, look at it and think about where it came from: the soil, the rain, the long road it traveled to reach you. If you pray, you can say a grace you already know, slowly, or thank God in your own words; if you don't, let the thanks rise anyway, to whoever it reaches.
For the life of the world. Alexander Schmemann's book, and his picture of humans as priests of creation, receiving the world and offering it back to God in thanks.
